name: Pedro Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Pedro, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Marta, who has a small roofing and repairs firm in our harbour town, four of us. Most of the work is old guesthouses on the seafront, the salt eats everything, so we're replacing rotten fascias, window frames, roof timbers, sometimes a whole dormer. I'm the trainee, at fifty-eight, which makes the young ones laugh, and I'm still not quick with a mitre. I was a deckhand on the ferries for twenty-eight years before this, so heights and weather don't bother me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you switch from the ferries?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They brought in newer ships with smaller crews, and the older deckhands were let go with a handshake and not much else. My son Erik's fishing boat went under around the same time and we paid off some of his debt, so savings are nearly nothing, maybe three weeks. My wife Helena works part-time at the fish plant. I use the AI on my phone every day, to check how to joint a timber, to help Marta write quotes, even to learn the names of things I've been calling 'the bit' for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, people just expected too much. On the group chat with my old ferry mates I'd say, look, it helps me every day, it's just not magic. At work I'd keep showing Marta how to do her quotes in half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays the same, which is fine but not great. I'm on low pay, I've got no savings, and the work is seasonal. AI staying small doesn't fix any of that, but it doesn't break anything either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it for learning and for Marta's paperwork, and I'd ask her for an extra hour's pay a week for doing the quotes. I'd try to finish my roofing certificate by next spring. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat, because I like seeing what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Marta for extra pay for the quotes. Would she agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if I show her the numbers. Last winter she lost two jobs because her quotes took a week, and since I started helping, she's had them out in a day. She's fair, she just doesn't like to be asked in front of the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the job for you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands. My head learns fast with the phone, but my hands are slow, and a mitre on a window frame either fits or it doesn't. The app can tell me the angle, it can't hold the saw straight.

S0.say: I'd say it's still useful, people just expected too much; it helps me every day but it's not magic. At work I'd keep showing Marta how to do her quotes in half the time.
S0.think: My life stays the same, which is fine but not great. Low pay, no savings and seasonal work don't get fixed by AI staying small, but nothing breaks either.
S0.do: Keeps using AI to learn the trade and handle Marta's paperwork, and asks for an extra hour's pay a week for doing quotes. Aims to finish his roofing certificate by next spring.
S0.feel: Calm, maybe a little flat because he likes seeing what's next.
S0.quote: Last winter she lost two jobs because her quotes took a week, and since I started helping, she's had them out in a day.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro is a late starter who is behind on hand skills but ahead on tools, and he's already turned that into value for his small firm. A stalled AI leaves his real problems, low and seasonal pay, untouched. He's practical and unbothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the kind of change you can ride if you get on early. I'd tell my old ferry mates not to make the mistake we made, waiting for the company to look after us. Online I'd share how I use the tools, because a lot of older guys are scared of them for no reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me, mostly. Small firms like Marta's will need someone who can work the new tools, and I'm already that person. The danger is the guesthouses themselves closing if travel changes, but that's not AI, that's just life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a cheap camera drone on a payment plan, maybe thirty a month, and offer roof checks to the guesthouses without anyone climbing a ladder. I'd learn whatever new measuring and planning apps come out, first in the firm. And I'd talk to Marta about making me the one who does surveys and quotes, so I'm not just the slow trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, even a little excited. Like the first time I steered the ferry in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A drone on a payment plan when you've got three weeks of savings. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, a bit. But I've watched Marta send someone up a ladder in the wind for an hour to look at one slipped slate. If the drone saves two climbs a month, she'd pay for that, and so would the guesthouse owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your old ferry mates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what I wish I'd done: learn something before the company decides for you. Half of them still sit in the harbour bar talking about the old ships. I'd send them a video of me flying the drone over a roof and say, if I can do it, you can.

S1.say: I'd say this is change you can ride if you get on early, and tell my old ferry mates not to wait for a company to look after them. I'd share online how I use the tools so older guys aren't scared.
S1.think: It's mostly good for me, because small firms like Marta's will need someone who can work the new tools, and I'm already that person. The bigger danger is guesthouses closing, which isn't AI.
S1.do: Buys a cheap camera drone on a payment plan of about thirty a month to offer roof checks without ladders. Learns new measuring and planning apps first and asks Marta to make him the surveys and quotes person.
S1.feel: Pretty calm, even a little excited.
S1.quote: I've watched Marta send someone up a ladder in the wind for an hour to look at one slipped slate.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro sees steady change as his opening: he would take a small, real money risk on a drone to make himself useful. His centre outlook shows in not blaming anyone and seeing travel trends as 'just life'. The ferry layoffs taught him not to wait for an employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody has to slow it down or soften it, the government, the companies, someone. I don't think anybody planned it to hurt us, it just runs ahead of everyone. I'd say people should get help while they find their feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd admit. I'm sixty in 2028, and if a robot can fix a fascia on a seafront guesthouse, Marta doesn't need four of us. I think I could be the one who runs the robots for her, but I might not be, and I've got no money to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Marta in the first month and say, when you buy a robot, let me be the one who looks after it, I'll learn everything. I'd cut what we can at home, the car's second insurance, eating out, and keep the drone checks going for cash. I'd study the robot makers' guides at night, the way I study roofing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd still feel like I had cards to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if Marta says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the bigger firms up the coast and say the same thing. I'd say I'm old, but I know roofs, I know the salt, I know the machines. Someone has to tell the robot which slate is the bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the drone side going straight away, not in a year. I'd ask Marta to send me on whatever robot course the makers offer, and I'd pay half if I had to. And I'd stop helping Erik with his loan, which would be a hard talk.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and someone has to slow it down or soften it, government or companies. Nobody planned it to hurt us, but people should get help while they find their feet.
S2.think: It worries me more than I'd admit. At sixty, if a robot can fix a fascia, Marta doesn't need four of us; I might be the one who runs the robots, but I've got no money to wait and see.
S2.do: Asks Marta in the first month to let him look after any robot she buys and studies the makers' guides at night. Cuts the second car insurance and eating out and keeps the drone roof checks going for cash.
S2.feel: Nervous, but still feeling he has cards to play.
S2.quote: Someone has to tell the robot which slate is the bad one.
S2.fieldNote: Even with two years and no savings, Pedro keeps looking for the role beside the machine rather than giving up. He's honest that his confidence is partly a front. His backup plan is to take the same pitch to bigger firms along the coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good warning and people should use it, not complain about it. I'd say government and the firms should pay for training older people on the machines. I'd tell anyone at the harbour cafe who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years suits me. I'd be sixty-three, with my roofing certificate and maybe a drone licence, and I'd have years on the tools already. I think I could make the switch to running inspections and robots before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a proper drone pilot licence in the first year, the course is a few hundred, and I'd pay it off in bits. I'd build up the roof check side job until it's bringing in maybe a hundred and fifty a month, and save every bit. And I'd keep learning the trade with Marta, because you can't check a robot's work if you don't know the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, because of money, but mostly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A licence and a reputation. With two, I'd be begging Marta for a chance. With five, the guesthouse owners already know me as the drone guy, and Marta needs me more than I need her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Helena agree to the money you'd spend on the licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd roll her eyes, she always does. Then she'd ask how much it brings back, and when I show her the guesthouse owners already asking, she'd say fine, but no new fishing rods this year. That's how it goes with us.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a good warning and people should use it, not complain. Government and firms should pay to train older people on the machines.
S3.think: Five years suits me. At sixty-three, with my roofing certificate and maybe a drone licence, I could switch to running inspections and robots before it lands.
S3.do: Gets a drone pilot licence in the first year, paying the course off in bits. Grows the roof check side job to about a hundred and fifty a month and saves it, while keeping up his trade training.
S3.feel: A bit uneasy about money, but mostly ready.
S3.quote: With five, the guesthouse owners already know me as the drone guy, and Marta needs me more than I need her.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Pedro time to build a licence and a reputation, which he sees as the key difference from two. He keeps trade skill at the centre: you can't check a robot's work without knowing the work. Money remains his main source of unease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and anyone who's still in the same spot in 2036 didn't try. Maybe that's harsh, people have their reasons. But I'd say get learning, the tools are free on your phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, at pension age, and by then I'd have years of drone inspections and maybe running Marta's machines behind me. I'm more worried about Erik out on his boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same as with five years, just without the rush. Get my roofing certificate, then the drone licence, build the side work slowly, save a bit each month. Maybe in five or six years help Marta choose which robot to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and curious to see what comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why worry about Erik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because fishing boats are already full of gadgets, and in ten years the boats might go out without anyone. He's thirty-four and he hates screens. I'd sit him down and show him what I've learned, whether he likes it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone still in the same spot in 2036 didn't try. Is that fair to someone like your ferry mates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, you're right, that's not fair. Some of them have bad hearts, bad backs, and a few can barely read. I'd take that back, it's easy for me to say with a phone in my hand every day.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone still in the same spot in 2036 didn't try, though maybe that's harsh. Get learning, the tools are free on your phone.
S4.think: I'd be fine, at sixty-eight and pension age with years of drone inspections and maybe Marta's machines behind me. I'm more worried about Erik on his fishing boat.
S4.do: Gets his roofing certificate, then the drone licence, and builds the side work slowly while saving a little each month. Plans to help Marta choose which robot to buy in five or six years.
S4.quote: He's thirty-four and he hates screens.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Pedro feels secure and his worry moves to his son, a fisherman who avoids screens. He catches himself being harsh about people who don't adapt and softens it. His plan is the same as with five years, only slower.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even if I'm quick, I've got no money to cover the gap while I find my place. What would help is a bit of income for a year while people retrain, and cheap courses for things like drone licences and robot servicing, aimed at people my age too, not just the young.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the old guys on the ferry did after. Most of them sat at home and waited for a call that never came. I promised myself I'd never wait like that again.

headlineQuote: I promised myself I'd never wait like that again.
portrait: Pedro Larsen is a 58-year-old trainee roofer at a small harbour-town firm, who came into building after twenty-eight years as a ferry deckhand. He's slow with a mitre but quick with AI, which he uses every day to learn the trade and write his boss's quotes. He stays calm through stalled and steady change, gets anxious with two-year AGI because he has no savings to bridge a gap, and sees five or ten years as time to become the local drone and robot inspection man. His worry with more time shifts to his son, a fisherman who hates screens.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because even moving fast he has no money to cover the gap while he finds his place.
whatWouldHelp: A year of income support while people retrain, and cheap courses such as drone licences and robot servicing open to older workers.
